newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian Socialists launch election campaign.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian Socialists launch election campaign.

text.p: Bulgaria's former ruling Socialist party, ousted last month by a campaign of mass street protests, gathered about 3,000 mainly elderly supporters on Thursday at the start of campaigning for April 19 elections.
Carrying red party flags and banners saying "Yes to agricultural cooperatives" and "No to destabilisation of the country", they braved freezing temperatures outside the National Palace of Culture.

"The Bulgarian Socialist Party has a long and rich history but still it is not a party of the past. We have our new ideas, organisations, new faces, which will form a strong group in the new national assembly," party leader Georgi Parvanov told the rally.
Elections were called 20 months ahead of schedule after 30 days of mass protests led by the Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) forced the ex-communist Socialists to stand down.
The UDF will launch its campaign on Saturday.
A total of 31 parties and coalitions will contest the poll, but only four or five have any chance of winning seats in the assembly.

All Bulgaria's political parties have pledged their support for a tough reform programme agreed by the interim cabinet and the International Monetary Fund to stabilise the shattered economy over the next year.

Both President Petar Stoyanov and interim prime minister Stefan Sofianski have warned the measures will be as painful as they are inevitable. Corruption and failure to implement reforms in the past seven years have brought the economy to the brink of collapse.

"Now we are facing a dramatic choice. Our opponents are suggesting that Bulgaria should join NATO but we support an independent, free and democratic Bulgaria which won't take part in any military bloc. In order to stop this, we have to win the elections," said Stefan Gaitandzhiev, leader of the small Socialist-allied Ecoglasnost party.
The interim cabinet has made a clear statement of its desire to join NATO, but the Socialists' manifesto calls for a referendum on the issue.

The Socialists won elections in December 1994 but lost support as the economy worsened. Their candidate suffered a decisive defeat in 1996 presidential elections won by Stoyanov, who ran on the ticket of the united opposition.
Former prime minister Zhan Videnov, who resigned as premier and Socialist party leader in December, will not be standing for election.
